title: Lost, or separated from your group: what to do (from the Army cold-weather and survival manuals)
asks: i am lost what do i do
lost in the woods what now
we got separated from our group
should i stay put or keep walking if lost
lost hiker what to do first
lost in a snowstorm with my group
do i stay where i am or try to walk out
im lost wat do i do
we are lost, no trail, getting dark, what do we do, over
answer: Keep calm and think clearly. Survival depends upon clear thinking and resourcefulness. Try to help each other.
Avoid making any decision immediately after it happens. If possible, wait until the shock has subsided, then evaluate the situation and decide.

If all is quiet and nothing guides you back to your group, go back to the last known position. If that is not possible, carefully consider the journey already made, and the distance and direction from the starting point.

If you are with others, gather information from the group. Send a search party to find the next known mark, marking its trail carefully so that it can return to guide the group forward or rejoin it. Meanwhile, the rest of the group should seek shelter.
If the search finds no known location: stay together. Meet the emergency as a group, do not wander off as individuals, and never let anyone straggle.
Take shelter. If a tent is available, set it up and get in. If there is no tent, build an improvised shelter. The type of shelter is not important if it protects from the weather.

Keep warm. If lost in a forest, light a fire. If lost where there are no trees, do not use a gasoline stove to heat the shelter: use it only to prepare hot food and drinks, conserve the fuel supply, and get into the sleeping bag to stay warm.
Check the food supply: collect all the food and water in the group and ration it systematically.

Check communications. If there is a radio, use it to call for help. In a forest, prepare fires to attract search planes: smoke is better by day and flame is better at night. Mirrors and ground signals help attract search parties.
Rest: less energy is expended. Eat while resting.
Watch each other for cold injury, using the buddy system. Watch for signs of frostbite and hypothermia.
If you are trapped in a vehicle in a winter storm, FEMA says to stay in your vehicle.

Where the authorities are in control and are willing and able to help recover you, that may favor staying near the place where you became isolated, at first. Consider moving only when you are certain that water, shelter, food and help can be reached, or when, after waiting several days, you are convinced that rescue is not coming and you are equipped to travel.
warnings: Moving is risky unless you have the necessities of survival. Leaving a safe shelter to travel in adverse weather is foolhardy, unless you are forced to escape.

quotes.text: Survival depends upon clear thinking and resourcefulness: Keep calm. Think. Try to help each other. Stay together. Keep warm.

Avoid making any decision immediately after the isolating event. If possible, wait a period to allow for recovery from the mental (if not the physical) shock resulting from the event. When shock has subsided, evaluate the situation, analyze the factors involved, and make valid decisions.

If all is quiet and there are no battle sounds or aircraft for guidance to friendly lines, go back to the last known position. If that is not possible, carefully consider the journey already made and the distance and direction from the starting point.

If with others, information should be gathered from the group. Send search parties out to find the next known steering mark. Carefully mark trails so the search party can return to guide the main group forward, or to rejoin the group should their search be unproductive. Meanwhile, the rest of the group should seek shelter. If the search party fails to find any known location, perform the steps below but remember to think clearly and keep calm:
Stay together: Meet the emergency as a group. Do not wander off as individuals, and never allow Soldiers to straggle.
Take shelter: If a tent is available, set it up and get in. If there is no tent, build an improvised shelter. The type of shelter is not important if there is protection from the weather.

Keep warm: If lost in a forest, light a fire (depending upon the enemy situation). If lost in an area where there are no trees, do not use the gasoline stove to heat the shelter. The stove is used only to prepare hot food and drinks. Conserve the fuel supply and get into the sleeping bag to stay warm.
Check the food supply: All food and water in the group is collected and rationed systematically.

Check communications: If there is a radio set, use it to contact the parent unit for help. If in a forest, prepare fires to attract search planes. Smoke is better by day and flame is better at night. Mirrors and ground signals are helpful in attracting search parties. Isolated Soldier guidance has ground and air signals for search planes. Rest: Less energy is expended. Food is eaten when resting.
Using the buddy system to watch for heat and cold injury.
Limit your time outside. If you need to go outside, wear layers of warm clothing. Watch for signs of frostbite and hypothermia. Avoid driving. If you are trapped, stay in your vehicle.

An operational environment in which host country military and law enforcement agencies have control as well as the intent and capability to assist recovery operations may favor staying near the isolation site (ex. aircraft crash) initially. Movement is considered only when certain that water, shelter, food, and help can be reached, or after having waited several days, they are convinced that recovery is not coming and they are equipped to travel.
Movement is risky unless the necessities of survival are available. To leave a safe shelter to travel in adverse weather conditions is foolhardy unless in an escape or evasion situation.

conflict: Stay or move: TC 21-3 (2025), written for a soldier separated from a unit in cold regions, says to 'go back to the last known position' when nothing guides you back. ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says to avoid making any decision immediately, that conditions may favor 'staying near the isolation site', and that 'Movement is considered only when certain that water, shelter, food, and help can be reached, or after having waited several days'. FEMA P-2064 (2020, winter storm) says 'If you are trapped, stay in your vehicle.' The card gives all three, in that order. No civilian search-and-rescue guidance for lost hikers is in the kit.
